title: You didn’t notice when it started. Nothing dramatic. No thunder. No sudden collapse. Just a quiet distance growing between you and God. Prayers felt thinner. Conviction felt quieter. And the things that once stirred your spirit… barely moved you now.
paragraphs: You didn’t notice when it started. Nothing dramatic. No thunder. No sudden collapse. Just a quiet distance growing between you and God. Prayers felt thinner. Conviction felt quieter. And the things that once stirred your spirit… barely moved you now.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
God doesn’t randomly withdraw. Distance is often the result of attitudes we protect.
And you’ve felt it.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.

The first one is pride, and it rarely looks like arrogance. It looks like self-justification. You explain away what God already called sin. You defend what the Spirit already convicted. You say, “I know, but…” and keep going.
Scripture cuts through that illusion: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” — James 4:6
Read that again.
Resists.
Not ignores. Not delays. Resists.
You felt that resistance when correction came and you pushed it away. God saw it. You knew.

Then comes disobedience, the quiet kind. Not rebellion that shocks people—but compromise that no one notices. Partial obedience dressed as faithfulness. You hear God clearly… and still choose differently.
Jesus said, “If you love Me, keep My commandments.” — John 14:15
Love isn’t what you say. It’s what you follow.
And that tension you feel? That inner unrest? It’s not confusion. It’s conflict between what you know and what you’re doing.
The third attitude is unforgiveness. And this one hides deep.
You replay what they did. You rehearse the pain. You carry the offense like it defines you. But forgiveness isn’t about them—it’s about your heart staying open before God.
Jesus warned plainly: “If you do not forgive others their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.” — Matthew 6:15
That’s not symbolic.
That’s a barrier.
You’ve asked God for mercy while withholding it from someone else. And something inside you knows that contradiction isn’t sustainable.
Then there’s love for the world. Not creation. Not people. But the system that pulls your heart away from God.
You crave what God said would destroy you. You entertain what once grieved you. And slowly, your appetite changes.

Scripture says, “Do not love the world or the things in the world… For all that is in the world—the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life—is not of the Father.” — 1 John 2:15–16
You didn’t fall overnight.
You drifted.
One compromise. One excuse. One moment at a time.
And now you feel it—that dullness where fire used to be.
The fifth attitude is indifference. This one is the most dangerous because it feels normal.
You’re not openly rejecting God. You’re just no longer pursuing Him. No urgency. No hunger. No fight for intimacy.
And Jesus spoke directly to this condition: “Because you are lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will vomit you out of My mouth.” — Revelation 3:16
That’s not distant theology.
That’s a warning.
Indifference doesn’t offend your comfort. It offends God.
And here’s the breaking point…
You can keep going like this—explaining, delaying, drifting—or you can face what’s real.
God hasn’t changed.
You have.
But this is where grace steps in, not to excuse you, but to restore you.
“Draw near to God and He will draw near to you.” — James 4:8
Not might.
Will.
But notice the order.
You draw near first.
Through repentance. Through surrender. Through honesty that stops pretending everything is fine.
This is the moment most people avoid. The silence right before change. The weight right before surrender.
You feel it now.
Two paths in front of you.
One keeps the attitudes. Keeps the distance. Keeps the slow drift until conviction fades completely.
The other breaks you—but heals you. Costs your pride—but restores your intimacy with God.
You already know which one is real.
Let it confront you.
If something in you is saying, “This is me,” don’t silence it.
Say it.
Confess it.
Turn from it.

And if this hit something deep, don’t keep it to yourself. Someone you know is living in that same quiet distance. Send this to them. Tag their name. Let truth reach them before numbness settles in deeper.
Follow this path if you’re done playing with distance and ready for real transformation. There’s more waiting—correction, depth, truth that will challenge and rebuild you.
And if you’re ready to go deeper, not just feel conviction but live changed, step into it:
Don’t wait for another moment like this.
This is the moment.
